newsitem.title: FRANCE: France praises Kohl amid fears it lagging Germany.
newsitem.headline: France praises Kohl amid fears it lagging Germany.

text.p: France on Wednesday praised Chancellor Helmut Kohl as Germany's longest-serving post-war leader in tributes that were tinged by fears that France is becoming overshadowed by its main European partner.

"Franco-German relations are good. They are fundamental for Europe, they must be intensified. That's the will of the two governments and the two peoples," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said when asked of Kohl's record.

Former European commission president Jacques Delors praised Kohl a friend and "man of vision" who reunited the country after the Cold War. The left-wing daily Liberation called him "The Colossus of Europe".

But Delors cautioned that Kohl's 14 years in office, surpassing Konrad Adenauer's 1949-63 record on Thursday, could be a symbol of German influence in Europe compared to a waning France racked by record unemployment and persistent gloom.

"We shouldn't develop a 'German syndrome' in France...or an inferiority complex. We have our own qualities...we must get out of this enormous doubt gripping French society," said Socialist Delors, who headed the Commission for 10 years until 1995.
"I don't think we should copy Germany but find our own path so that our historical and traditional qualities overcome our classic weaknesses," he told Europe 1 radio.
"Germany will absolutely need France for years to come, psychologically, politically and even economically," he said.

The French daily Le Monde said the Franco-German partnership at the heart of the European Union may lost some of its intensity even as the two are trying to revive their economies to stay in step for a single European currency from 1999.

Paris irked Bonn with nuclear tests in the South Pacific and with a trip last week by President Jacques Chirac to the Middle East to push for a European role in peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians.
"Seen from Bonn, the personal relationship between Helmut Kohl and Jacques Chirac is not as intense as with (late French president) Francois Mitterrand," it said.
"It's certain that the Germany of Helmut Kohl thinks like France: it's even one of the guiding lines of its foreign policy. But it would often like France to think like Germany," Le Monde said.

Chirac's first foreign policy act after taking office in 1995 was to have dinner with Kohl in the eastern French city of Strasbourg, in a region that has switched back and forth to German and French control in three wars since 1870.
